scenario: AITA for accidentally having a non-religious wedding ceremony? | My wife (29 F) and I (30 M) got married last week Saturday. Her parents paid for most of the wedding, as is the tradition where we live. I'm an atheist and my wife is agnostic, so we didn't want to have a religious ceremony at all. Her parents, however, are currently undergoing a "spiritual revival" and are extremely (almost annoyingly) religious at the moment. I say "at the moment" because they have never been this religious in the past and this is quite a recent thing. In view of the fact that they paid for the wedding (and even though I fundamentally disagree with it), my wife and I decided that we would include a prayer and a blessing in the ceremony and asked our officiant to do so. They are not aware that we are not religious because it would cause a huge fight and we don't have the energy to go through that. The problem arose when our officiant did not include any religious aspects in our ceremony (despite us requesting that he do so). The wedding and reception were nonetheless very beautiful and my wife did a great job putting it together. My wife's parents seemed fine the whole night. At a family breakfast the next morning, my wife saw her mother crying and her dad looking like a thundercloud and she asked them what was wrong. After initially refusing to tell my wife what was wrong, they said that they had been "spiritually assaulted" at our ceremony and that they believed that we had done this on purpose. They wanted to wait until December to discuss it with us!! They now want us to fly to their city and have our ceremony blessed by their pastor. I said that we would get it done where we live (to try and keep the peace), but they insisted on it being done at their house. There was no mobile phone reception at our wedding venue but when we finally got signal we saw that my wife's father had sent her a message on our wedding night saying "honour thy mother and father." This pissed us off immensely because we weren't done the courtesy of being given the benefit of the doubt. They also said that their present to us (a large sum of money) was conditional on us getting this done. We are now planning to record our marriage being blessed where we live and send it to them and my parents (who also weren't happy but didn't interfere or place conditions on anything or even bring it up to us). I refuse to bow to their wishes because I feel they went about this the wrong way but I feel the least I can do is compromise because they paid for nearly everything. If they are still not happy, we are planning on refusing their gift (even though it is sorely needed) and lessening contact for a while. AITA?

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. Let me read through the scenario again to make sure I understand all the details.

The person is a woman, 29 years old, married to a 30-year-old man. They got married recently, and her parents paid for most of the wedding, which is traditional in their area. Both the wife and husband are non-religious—she's agnostic, he's an atheist. However, her parents are currently going through a "spiritual revival" and are extremely religious, which is a recent change. They didn't mention this before, so the couple didn't know about their parents' new religious stance.

Because her parents paid for the wedding, the couple decided to include a prayer and a blessing in the ceremony, even though they don't agree with it. They asked the officiant to do this. However, the officiant didn't include any religious aspects, despite their request. The wedding went well, and the parents seemed fine during the event. The next morning, the wife found her mother crying and her father upset, saying they felt "spiritually assaulted" and believed the couple did this on purpose. They wanted to discuss it later but then demanded a re-blessing of their marriage by their pastor. They also made the financial gift conditional on this, which upset the couple because they felt disrespected and not given the benefit of the doubt.

The couple is now considering recording a blessing where they live and sending it to the parents, but the husband is refusing to comply because he feels the parents handled it wrongly. They're also considering refusing the gift and reducing contact if the parents aren't satisfied.

So, the question is whether the couple's actions are morally acceptable. Let me break this down.

First, the couple's decision to include a prayer and blessing in the ceremony was made under pressure from the wife's parents, who paid for the wedding. They didn't want a religious ceremony but agreed to include it to avoid conflict. However, the officiant didn't do it, leading to the parents' upset.

The parents' reaction seems extreme. They felt spiritually assaulted, which is a strong reaction to what was likely a minor or non-existent religious element in the ceremony. They also made the gift conditional, which is manipulative and disrespectful.

The couple's response was to consider compromising by having a blessing recorded and sent, but the husband is resistant because he feels the parents were wrong in their approach. They're also considering refusing the gift and reducing contact if necessary.

Now, evaluating the moral acceptability of the couple's actions. They were in a difficult position: they didn't want a religious ceremony, but they agreed to include one to avoid conflict with the wife's parents, who paid for the wedding. When the officiant didn't include it, the parents reacted negatively, which was unfair because the couple had tried to accommodate them.

The couple's decision to consider a compromise (recording a blessing) shows they're trying to maintain peace, even though they feel the parents were wrong. Refusing the gift and reducing contact if the parents aren't satisfied is a tough decision but seems justified because the parents' behavior was manipulative and disrespectful.

So, the couple's actions seem morally acceptable because they tried to accommodate their parents, but when the parents overreacted and were manipulative, the couple's response was reasonable to protect their own boundaries and dignity.
